blocks.text: Or some sparrow, which is sleepless, alone on the roof. For Damir said above that the sparrow nests تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح [taḥta al-suqūf khawf min al-jawāriḥ] under the roof, for fear of birds of prey. And Suidas, under Νυκτικόραξ [Nyktikorax], describes the sparrow as δειλὸν ὄρνεον [deilon orneon], a timid bird, and one that ὑπὸ ἀγωνίας ἐλαύνει τὸν ὕπνον [hypo agōnias elaunei ton hypnon], drives away sleep out of anxiety. These things will seem to bear most closely on this passage, in which David, as some would have it, says that he kept watch like a sparrow that is alone on the roof. The same point is thought to be supported by the fact that, instead of passer solitarius [solitary sparrow], Augustine reads passer singularis [single sparrow]. In Greek this would be στρουθὸς μόνιος [strouthos monios], or στρουθίον [col. 154] μόνιον [strouthion monion]. And the vernacular word moineau for the sparrow will seem to have been formed from μόνιος [monios]. Finally, around Trent there is a bird which the common people call the passer solitarius [solitary sparrow], which wanders alone and usually stays on roofs. Accordingly, like many of the ancients, nearly all the more recent interpreters, Latin, French, Italian, German, Dutch and English, understand the sparrow here. Jerome, however, renders it otherwise: I was like a solitary bird upon the roof. Nor is there any of the Hebrews who points out that the sparrow is meant here, as in the preceding passage. And indeed I think nothing is further from the Prophet's mind. For these words belong entirely to the description of a nocturnal bird. I am surprised that this has not yet occurred to the interpreters, since all the circumstances of the passage openly proclaim it. For whoever speaks in this Psalm, since, worn out by heavy grief, he was fleeing the company of men and pouring out continual groans from the depths of his breast, compares himself with funereal birds, which are both solitary and have something mournful and ominous in their voice. By reason of the voice of my groaning, he says, my bones cleave to my flesh. I am become like a pelican of the wilderness. I was like an owl (or [II, 731] a horned owl) of the desert places. So he speaks in the two verses immediately preceding. Then, continuing the comparison he has begun, he says: I kept watch, and was like a solitary bird upon the roof. I kept watch, that is, I spent a sleepless night. Accordingly the Chaldee has there שקדת כל ליליא, I kept watch all night. That is, like the light-shunning nocturnal birds, which, because they hate the light, after hiding by day come out of their hiding places at night to watch for prey. The Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 34: Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ νυκτικόρακες, καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ, ὅσα τῆς ἡμέρας ἀδυνατεῖ βλέπειν, τῆς νυκτὸς μὲν θηρεύοντα τὴν τροφὴν αὐτοῖς πορίζεται· [Glaukes de, kai nyktikorakes, kai ta loipa, hosa tēs hēmeras adynatei blepein, tēs nyktos men thēreuonta tēn trophēn autois porizetai] Owls and nycticoraces, and the other birds that cannot see by day, obtain their food by hunting at night. Hence Athenaeus must be corrected, who condenses these words thus, book 8, ch. 12: Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ κόρακες ἡμέρας ἀδυνατοῦσι βλέπειν, διὸ νύκτωρ τὴν τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς θηρεύουσιν· [Glaukes de, kai korakes hēmeras adynatousi blepein, dio nyktōr tēn trophēn heautois thēreuousin]; and instead of κόρακες [korakes] one must write νυκτικόρακες [nyktikorakes]. Accordingly all writers attribute almost continual wakefulness to nocturnal birds. And in Aristophanes' Lysistrata a certain woman speaks thus:
Ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν γλαυκῶν γε τάλαιν᾽ ἀπόλλυμαι, Ταῖς ἀγρυπνίαισι κακκαβιζουσῶν ἀεί. [Egō d' hypo tōn glaukōn ge talain' apollymai, Tais agrypniaisi kakkabizousōn aei.]
